meta.source: Recomputed from the published data files of six pages in the Evidence Room, PIC’s public data archive: wages, concentration, occupations, federal money, the funding map and revisions.
meta.sources: Behind those pages: annual average employment and wages from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, the count the Bureau of Labor Statistics builds from state unemployment-insurance filings; BLS Employment Projections and completed degrees from IPEDS, the federal survey every college reports to; award and contract records from USAspending, filed against the place of performance the award names; the signed award documents themselves; and archived earlier releases of the price series from ALFRED, the Federal Reserve’s archive of what each statistic said on the day it was published.
meta.row: One row is one measure in one year: its level, the baseline it is read against, and every year-over-year change the same measure has made in its published history.
meta.definition: How far a measure usually moves is worked out the same way for all five. Take the measure’s own published history, compute the change between every consecutive pair of years, hold out the latest one, and compare it against the median and the largest of the earlier changes. A move at or below the median is an ordinary year for that measure, which by construction about half of years are; a move larger than every earlier one has no precedent in the series.
meta.baseline: Each tile states the baseline it is read against and why that one. PIC has set no target for any of these five measures, so no tile reports distance from a target: they report level and direction only.
meta.caution: What is measured here is how far a published series has moved between years. That is not the same as how far a future revision will move the year just published, which this repository has measured for exactly three producer-price indexes (the prices factories charge for their output), on the revisions page, and for none of the employment, degree or spending series here.
meta.suppression: A county figure the bureau withholds is never a zero. Three of the five measures are built from one figure per county per industry, and the set the bureau publishes changes year to year, so for those three the movement is judged on the figures present in every year rather than on the raw total.
meta.scope: The three industries counted here are the census codes for resin and synthetic rubber (3252), paint and coatings (3255) and plastics and rubber products (326). The wider chemicals code 325 sweeps in pharmaceuticals, agricultural chemicals and industrial gas, about 60 percent of its own figure, and is context rather than cluster.
meta.not: This page carries no measure of output, productivity, exports, private investment or company formation, because no page in this room ships one yet. Five measures are not the health of an economy.
meta.geography: Every employment, wage and contracting figure is on the twelve counties PIC treats as its region. The degree completions are three named universities and the openings estimate beside them is a state projection for an eighteen-county region: they are printed side by side and never divided into one another.

series: PPI: plastics and rubber products manufacturing

tiles.question: How many jobs is this?
tiles.reading: 24,030 jobs in the three industries the cluster measures itself by, counted across the twelve counties in 2025. It is a floor rather than a total: the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes one figure per county per industry, and it withheld 12 of the 36 to keep single employers unidentifiable.
tiles.means: On the 21 county figures published in every year since 2015, the only run that holds the same set of counties still, the total went 25,281 in 2023, then 24,259, then 23,457. That is the third straight fall, and fewer jobs is the bad direction here.

baseline.name: the same county figures in 2024
baseline.why: A year is the shortest step this series takes, and comparing the same set of counties is the only way to hold the measurement frame still while the economy moves.

direction.words: down 802 jobs, 3.3 percent, on the county figures published in both years
direction.of: on the county figures published in both years

tiles.blind: 12 of the 36 county-by-industry figures are withheld so no employer can be identified from them. A withheld figure is not a zero, and the jobs behind it are not in the 24,030.

vintage.changes_it: The Bureau of Labor Statistics revises these county figures, which come from its Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, when employers refile. A new annual release replaces this figure outright.

tiles.question: Is this cluster unusual, or just present?
tiles.reading: Paint and coatings is the most concentrated of the three: these twelve counties hold about six times the share of it that the country does. Plastics and rubber, the industries the region is known for, run 2.32 times.
tiles.means: A high share cuts both ways. Six times the country’s concentration is what makes these counties worth a buyer’s flight, and it is what ties local payroll to one industry’s cycle. This year’s fall moves them a step toward looking like the country, which costs some of each.

baseline.name: 1.0 times, the national share of employment
baseline.why: A share against the country needs no peer region chosen for it and no target set for it, and PIC has set none. At 1.0 the counties look like the country; above it they hold more of this work than their size implies.

direction.words: down from 6.40× to 5.96× the national share, a fall of 0.44

tiles.blind: Five of the twelve counties are withheld for paint and coatings, so this is a reading on the seven that report. The withheld ones are the small ones, which are usually the least concentrated.

vintage.changes_it: A county entering or leaving disclosure moves the composite without any employer changing what it does.

tiles.question: Are these good jobs?

value_parts.k: the average job in its own county
the same industry across the country

tiles.reading: The typical polymer job out-pays the average job in its own county by 1.24 times, and pays 0.90 times what the same industry averages nationally. Both are true at once, and 15 of the 24 published county figures, holding 12,896 of the 24,030 jobs, sit in both states.

baseline.name: two baselines, because one of them flatters
baseline.why: Against the county average it answers whether this is good work to have here; against the same industry nationally, whether this is a good place to do it. A recruiting number that carries only the first is choosing the flattering half.

direction.words: the national side rose from 0.861× to 0.895× of the U.S. rate for the same work
direction.of: on the year, on the national side

drivers.label: Beats its own county
drivers.note: median 1.24 times the county all-industry average

drivers.label: Beats its industry nationally
drivers.note: median 0.90 times the U.S. average for the same work

drivers.label: Weekly wage per covered job
drivers.note: against $1,505 for the same industry mix nationally

tiles.blind: An average weekly wage moves with hours and with the mix of occupations as much as with pay rates: a plant on overtime reads as a raise. Nothing here is any one person’s pay.

vintage.changes_it: The local ratio has no published history here, so only the national side can be judged against its own past. A year of wage revisions moves both.

tiles.question: Who is coming out of the schools?
tiles.reading: The three universities in the region conferred 63 polymer degrees in 2023, against 179 in 2016, their own high. Materials degrees, the other group of programs these three schools count here, held at 33.

baseline.name: the same three institutions in 2016, their own high
baseline.why: A peer region would need a defensible peer set and PIC has named none. The programs’ own decade is the baseline that needs no choice made for it.

direction.words: up 9 on the year, and 65 percent below its 2016 high

tiles.question: Is public money arriving, and where does it land?
tiles.reading: $51.0 million of the $54.1 million in federal awards on the funding map is written into signed awards naming seven organizations. None of it is disbursement: every figure here is money committed, not money spent.
tiles.means: A bigger number here is good news for the region only once the money is spent, and no figure on this page tracks spending. Read $51.0M as a queue with seven names on it. The change printed beside it, up $16.4M, belongs to a different series: the year-on-year move in routine contracting, money already flowing to plants here.

baseline.name: routine federal contracting, $36.6 million a year in 2025 dollars
baseline.why: An award is only large or small against the money that was already arriving. Averaged over the seven closed fiscal years, FY2019 to FY2025; FY2026 is still open and is left out of the average.

direction.words: routine contracting rose to $39.0M in FY2025 from $22.5M, 73 percent higher
direction.of: in routine contracting on the year, which is not the $51.0M above

drivers.label: The award, in years of routine contracting

tiles.blind: The contracting series filters on manufacturing industry codes, so university and research awards are invisible to it: a $15.0M National Science Foundation Engines award appears in no figure here. Place of performance is a field reported on the award, not an observation of where work happened.
